beats.t: A week passed. Yeoni's search history filled with names beginning with Park. Park Minsu, Park Junho, Park Seonghun. None right.
Searching only Parks will never end. Better find another clue.
The notebook's last page had gained more lines. Park-whatever. Possibly white hair. Obsessed with socks. Sensitive about star ratings.
That's all my clues? If I were a detective, I'd be fired.
Still, the bad luck had truly stopped. Toast fell butter-side up; buses arrived on time. Yeoni felt a little wistful about it.
Good luck is nice. But there's no one to tease.
Yeoni left a cushion in the empty place at the foot of the bed. Every morning they looked at it, and every morning felt a little foolish.
A thud came from outside the door, followed by something spilling. Yeoni slipped on their slippers and opened up.
Potting soil scattered the hallway. Seo Hanbi knelt in the middle, a new plant pot in each hand.
Oh. Was that loud? I'm sorry.
What's all this?
The lady in 302's pots. I broke them that day. With my tiger tail.
Yeoni remembered. The night black hands reached from the phone. A black tiger racing across the hallway. The place its tail had swept.
You remembered that?
I wrote everything down. Not in a ledger. Just a notebook.
Neat handwriting lined the notebook she offered. Some entries ended in a small circle. Others were unchecked.
[ Two plant pots, 302 ○ · Hallway window ○ · Twelve convenience-store umbrellas · Security-office chair · And Yeoni ]
What's the last line? I'm not an object.
I don't know when I'll be able to circle that one. It's the biggest line.
Yeoni couldn't find words. Seo Hanbi began scooping soil with her hands. Beneath her nails, black dirt gathered, at odds with her elegant politeness.
I'll help. Let me get a broom.
No, this is mine to...
Insisting on cleaning the dirt alone is stubbornness. Repayment and stubbornness are different.
They swept in silence. The door to 302 opened. The elderly woman saw the new pots and widened her eyes.
I'm the one who broke them. I'm sorry.
She looked at Seo Hanbi for a long time, then pressed one pot back into her hands.
She says keep one. Your room looks like it has no greenery.
I shouldn't accept.
Practice receiving too. Like the bread.
Seo Hanbi held the pot in both hands. She looked as lost as she had before bread offered at no price. Then she gave a small bow.
Thank you. I'll take good care of it. Truly, this time.
How will you repay twelve convenience-store umbrellas? Tiger tail again?
Claws that time. So I've arranged to work there. Night shifts. I asked them to deduct the umbrellas from my wages.
The owner agreed?
He called me strange. But he took me on. There are more people willing to accept strange people than I expected.
After saying it, Seo Hanbi looked slightly surprised, as though amazed those words had come from her own mouth.
That afternoon, a new tent stood outside the campus gate. Its handwritten sign read: Compatibility readings. First session free. Birth time unknown? I'll work it out.
This man. Honestly.
Customer, birth date and time first. Oh, Yeoni. Free customers aren't my favorite.
It says first session free.
Yours isn't the first. I read you fifty times over there.
Kang Saebyeok. The man called Yundal in the world of destiny. He no longer wore gloves. His palm held ordinary lines.
Do people remember you now?
Yesterday a regular called my name. 'Saebyeok.' I almost cried on the spot.
I called Mom too. Her first words were, 'Have you eaten?' After three years.
What did you say?
Lied and said yes. Family tradition.
Yeoni laughed and sat in a tent chair. Yundal—no, Saebyeok—opened his perpetual calendar without asking.
How's Hanbi? Doing well?
Sweeping soil in the hallway. Carrying a notebook.
Atonement her way. A notebook instead of a ledger. A good upgrade.
Aren't you bored without Mr. Cat? You fought every day.
Honestly, a little. Without anyone getting jealous, reading your palm isn't as fun.
You're looking for a Park, I hear. Among four million of them.
How do you know?
You walk around holding your phone with your search history visible. Half of divination is observation.
Saebyeok pointed to Yeoni's chart: Year Im-o, Month Byeong-o, Day Eulhae, Hour Gyeong-Chen. All eight spaces filled.
Gyeong has returned. The severed connection is restored. It could be a clue to finding him.
Stop using that expression.
Looking at this week's yearly influence: an eastern waterside. Before the blossoms fall. Where a helpful person stands.
Eastern waterside means the river. Do you know how many kilometers of riverbank Seoul has?
Find the rest with your legs. A reading gives direction. The rest is footwork.
Yeoni stopped as they stood. Dark clouds gathered outside the tent. Saebyeok glanced at the sky.
And rain this evening. Take an umbrella. An extra one too.
Six in the evening. A sudden shower poured down. Yeoni opened their yellow umbrella and ran beneath the bus-stop roof. The umbrella with three layers of tape.
Someone stood at the roof's edge without an umbrella, one shoulder half wet. Seo Hanbi.
Hanbi. Your umbrella?
I don't have one. The black umbrella vanished with the ring. It was never mine.
Rain drummed on the roof. The bus didn't come. They stood side by side, watching traffic lights spread across puddles.
It was here. Where you shared your umbrella with me in the first spring. This bus stop.
I don't remember.
I know. That made me glad. Because you didn't know that spring, I could begin repaying you from the start.
Yeoni tilted the umbrella halfway over Seo Hanbi's wet shoulder. Their own left shoulder soaked in the rain.
Don't. If you do, I...
I know. You said I did this then too.
Seo Hanbi's face crumpled. Not into the collapse of madness. More like someone who had held on for a long time finally sitting down.
Yeoni. I have no right to ask forgiveness.
Black Moon deceived me, but the hand that collected your fortune was mine. I shouldn't accept this umbrella with that hand.
I know. That's why I want to decide.
Yeoni adjusted their grip on the umbrella. Rain ran in lines from its edge.
You've repaid the pots. The window too. The twelve umbrellas aren't done. Keep repaying those.
Yes.
But separately from that, I forgive you now. I've decided.
Seo Hanbi looked at Yeoni like someone who didn't understand, then someone who did. She took one long breath.
Can you decide so easily?
It wasn't easy at all. I thought about it all week. Between searching for Parks.
Between?
The Park search is the main event. Sorry.
Seo Hanbi laughed aloud with a wet face. It was the first time Yeoni heard her laugh aloud then.
The rain thinned. Sunset leaked between the clouds. Wet asphalt glittered orange.
May I ask one thing? We made a promise that spring.
The sea?
You remember?
No. You told me. The day you returned the umbrella, after the water cleared.
You remembered that?
I wrote it in my notebook. Right above Park-whatever.
Yeoni swiped through the phone calendar. After cherry blossoms, before the rainy season. One square was empty.
Second Saturday in May. Let's go to the sea. I'll make gimbap.
Then I'll buy umbrellas. Two. With my own money this time.
[ App notification · Moka: Going to the sea? Without me? Prepare for bad reviews. ]
How did he know?
I think the universe tattled.
The bus came. Seo Hanbi boarded first. Folding the umbrella, Yeoni saw something across the street.
The road toward the river. Beneath a cherry tree still holding blossoms, a man's back as he folded a white umbrella. A strand of hair caught the light and looked white.
Oh.
The man sneezed. Seeing a stray cat pass his feet, he stepped back, like someone allergic to cat fur.
The bus doors closed. Yeoni pressed a palm to the window. The man walked east, toward the river.
Yeoni? What's wrong? Someone you know?
No idea. A stranger. But that sneeze...
Yeoni couldn't finish. They pulled out the notebook and hurriedly wrote beneath the last line: White umbrella. Cat allergy. Toward the river.
Eastern waterside. Before the blossoms fall.
